title: When the Weather Wakes
premise: Theo Joubert, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost her sense of taste after her mother's death, finds a box of forty undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe in her late mother's house — letters her mother wrote to a man wrongfully imprisoned decades ago in their coastal hometown of Verre-sur-Mer. As Theo delivers them one by one, she uncovers a miscarriage of justice the town has spent thirty years burying, and discovers her own father helped bury it. Torn between protecting her family's name and giving a dying man his truth, Theo must return to Verre-sur-Mer before her own memories of her mother dissolve entirely; she ends by publishing the story under her mother's name, testifying at the reopened inquiry, and finally tasting food again — bitter first, then sweet.
about_author: Wendell Coldharbour is the pen name of a former court reporter who spent a decade covering wrongful convictions before turning to fiction. He writes from a farmhouse on the Atlantic coast, where he claims the weather keeps better minutes than any stenographer.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Theo: a Michelin-starred dinner she cannot taste, a review written entirely from texture and memory, and an editor's warning that her prose has gone cold. Emotional beat: elegant numbness masking grief.

chapters.title: Forty Envelopes Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Clearing her mother's house, Theo pries loose a wardrobe panel and finds a box of sealed, stamped, never-mailed letters addressed to 'A. Ferreira, HMP Wolds.' POV: Theo. Beat: shock curdling into compulsion — she reads the first letter standing in the dust.

chapters.title: What My Mother Never Sent
chapters.summary: The first letter, reproduced in full: her mother confessing she saw something the night of the fire in Verre-sur-Mer, 1991. Theo cross-checks dates against her childhood. Beat: the ground tilts; the mother she knew becomes a stranger.

chapters.title: Verre-sur-Mer Smells Like Salt and Secrets
chapters.summary: Theo drives to the coastal town she fled at nineteen. The chippy is gone; the courthouse remains. A former neighbor pretends not to know her. Beat: dread braided with homesickness.

chapters.title: The Man Who Kept the Lighthouse Ledger
chapters.summary: She tracks down Silas Renard, retired harbormaster, who kept unofficial records of that night. He warns her off: 'Some verdicts are load-bearing, girl.' Beat: first open resistance; the town closes ranks.

chapters.title: Letter Two: The Fire at the Ferry Hotel
chapters.summary: Her mother describes the blaze that killed hotelier Marguerite Osei and put Aldo Ferreira away for arson and manslaughter. Theo pulls the trial coverage from the library microfiche. Beat: forensic curiosity hardening into doubt.

chapters.title: Aldo Ferreira Is Dying
chapters.summary: Theo visits the prison hospice. Ferreira, frail and lucid, assumes she's press until she says her surname — Joubert. His face changes. Beat: confrontation without accusation; he asks only, 'Did she ever forgive herself?'

chapters.title: What the Town Agreed to Forget
chapters.summary: In the pub, Theo hears the official version recited like liturgy. An old fisherman, drunk, mutters that the fire started before Ferreira's boat even docked. Beat: the crack in the consensus widens.

chapters.title: Letter Seven: The Witness Who Was Twelve
chapters.summary: Her mother admits she was the child witness whose testimony convicted Ferreira — coached, she now believes, by someone she won't name. Theo realizes her mother carried this for thirty years. Beat: grief reorganized around betrayal.

chapters.title: My Father's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Sorting estate papers, Theo recognizes her father's handwriting on a 1991 police liaison memo — he wasn't just a local solicitor; he advised the investigation. Beat: the family vault opens; nausea and clarity arrive together.

chapters.title: The Editor's Offer
chapters.summary: Back in London, Theo pitches the story as investigative memoir. Her editor smells a career-defining piece but warns: accuse a dead town and a dead father, and there's no walking it back. Beat: ambition wrestling loyalty.

chapters.title: Letter Thirteen: Love, Undelivered
chapters.summary: A letter reveals her mother and Ferreira were lovers before the fire — the letters are half confession, half love never allowed to finish. Beat: Theo's image of her parents' marriage fractures; tenderness complicates judgment.

chapters.title: Silas Breaks His Silence
chapters.summary: Renard shows Theo his ledger: tide tables proving the ferry docked ninety minutes after the fire began. He gives her a photocopy and makes her promise to be careful. Beat: alliance formed; hope with teeth.

chapters.title: The Osei Family Still Lights a Candle
chapters.summary: Theo meets Grace Osei, daughter of the victim, who has spent her life believing justice was served. Theo leaves without telling her why she came. Beat: guilt — truth-telling will wound the innocent too.

chapters.title: Someone Goes Through the Box
chapters.summary: Returning to the house, Theo finds the wardrobe panel replaced and two letters missing. Footprints in the flowerbed. Beat: paranoia arrives; the stakes turn physical.

chapters.title: Letter Twenty-One: The Name She Wouldn't Write
chapters.summary: A letter names the fire's likely true origin — an insurance scheme involving the hotel's silent partner — but the signature line is torn away. Beat: so close, and robbed; fury sharpens method.

chapters.title: The Silent Partner Had a Son
chapters.summary: Theo identifies the partner: Edmund Vasse, dead, whose son Charles still owns half the seafront. Charles Vasse is charming, generous, and suddenly very interested in her research. Beat: the antagonist enters wearing a smile like hers.

chapters.title: Dinner With the Devil
chapters.summary: Vasse hosts Theo at his restaurant; she catalogues every dish she cannot taste while he offers to fund her 'memoir' — provided it stays literary, not legal. Beat: temptation dressed as kindness; she recognizes her own deflection technique used on her.

chapters.title: Letter Twenty-Six: Run
chapters.summary: Her mother's most desperate letter urges Ferreira to appeal, then retracts it — 'They know about us. They will use you.' Theo maps the timeline: her mother was threatened. Beat: fear inherited across time.

chapters.title: Grace Reads Letter Nine
chapters.summary: Unable to carry it alone, Theo shows Grace Osei the letter describing what her mother truly saw. Grace's world cracks; she slaps Theo, then asks to see the rest. Beat: betrayal transmuting into partnership — the victim's daughter joins the search.

chapters.title: The Courthouse Basement
chapters.summary: With Grace's help, Theo accesses archived evidence: the accelerant report was downgraded, a second set of fingerprints unlogged. Someone with legal access sanitized the file. Beat: documentary proof; the case turns real.

chapters.title: My Father's Confession, Drafted and Never Sent
chapters.summary: In his old office safe, Theo finds her father's unsent confession letter — he buried the anomaly to protect her pregnant mother from prosecution as a perjuring witness. Beat: devastating motive; love as the engine of injustice.

chapters.title: Vasse Makes It Explicit
chapters.summary: Charles Vasse threatens Theo: publish, and he'll paint her mother as the arsonist's accomplice and destroy Ferreira's appeal anyway. He returns the two stolen letters — altered. Beat: the villain's full weight lands; isolation presses in.

chapters.title: The Taste Returns Wrong
chapters.summary: At a roadside café, Theo abruptly tastes her tea — metallic, unpleasant. The psychogenic numbness is lifting as the truth surfaces. Beat: body and conscience reconnecting; healing begins as damage.

chapters.title: Letter Thirty-Three: What Forgiveness Isn't
chapters.summary: Her mother writes that forgiveness without truth is just forgetting with better manners. Theo drafts her article and deletes it twice. Beat: the theme stated; courage not yet found.

chapters.title: Ferreira Stops Eating
chapters.summary: The hospice calls: Ferreira has begun refusing food, done waiting. Theo races to read him the letters aloud — all forty — over three days. Beat: race against death; the letters finally delivered by mouth if not by post.

chapters.title: 'Tell Them I Was Here'
chapters.summary: Ferreira, hearing everything, asks only that the record show who he was before 1991: a cook, a brother, a man who loved her mother. He signs an affidavit. Beat: dignity reclaimed; the moral center holds.

chapters.title: The Town Finds Out
chapters.summary: A local paper runs Theo's inquiry application on its front page. Verre-sur-Mer splits: threats on her door, but also anonymous notes confirming details — the town's silence was always many silences. Beat: the dam breaks both ways.

chapters.title: Silas Pays for the Ledger
chapters.summary: Renard's shed is burned; he survives, hospitalized, and tells Theo he expected it since 1991. Beat: cost made flesh; Theo's resolve stops being optional.

chapters.title: Letter Forty: To My Daughter, If You're Reading
chapters.summary: The final letter is addressed to Theo herself: her mother knew she'd find the box, and begs her to choose truth over inheritance — 'You were always the one who tasted everything.' Beat: benediction; the mission becomes love.

chapters.title: The Article Under Her Mother's Byline
chapters.summary: Theo publishes the full investigation in a long-form piece credited jointly to her mother's name and her own. National outlets pick it up; the Criminal Cases Review Commission announces a referral. Beat: the point of no return, crossed deliberately.

chapters.title: Vasse's Counterattack
chapters.summary: Vasse sues for defamation and leaks the love letters to frame her mother as a liar. Theo, prepared, releases the unaltered originals and the torn-signature forensics. Beat: climax's opening movement; she fights in daylight now.

chapters.title: The Hearing at the Royal Courts
chapters.summary: At the CCRC hearing, Theo testifies about the letters, the ledger, and her father's confession. Grace Osei speaks for the truth despite her grief. Beat: climax — private grief offered up as public testimony.

chapters.title: The Verdict on Vasse
chapters.summary: Newly surfaced insurance documents and a deathbed statement from a retired firefighter unravel Vasse's position; criminal investigators open a file on the 1991 cover-up. Beat: the load-bearing verdict removed; the town exhales.

chapters.title: Conviction Quashed
chapters.summary: Ferreira's conviction is quashed in a hospital-room ruling; he dies nine days later, exonerated, holding the forty letters. Beat: bittersweet apex — justice arrives, late, and it is still justice.

chapters.title: The Funeral She Plans Herself
chapters.summary: Theo buries the letters with Ferreira at his request, keeping copies, and scatters nothing of her mother — instead planting a garden behind the wardrobe wall. Beat: mourning completed rather than deferred.

chapters.title: Eating in Verre-sur-Mer
chapters.summary: Theo eats breakfast at the rebuilt chippy: egg, chips, strong tea — and tastes all of it, weeping quietly into the vinegar. Beat: the wound's purpose revealed; taste restored by truth.

chapters.title: The Book Deal and the Refusal
chapters.summary: Publishers circle; Theo agrees to write the book but refuses to let it become entertainment, insisting proceeds go to the Osei family and Ferreira's exonerees' fund. Beat: integrity chosen over appetite; belonging redefined.

chapters.title: What the Weather Wakes
chapters.summary: One year on, Theo leads a writing workshop in Verre-sur-Mer for townspeople telling their own buried stories. Storm season opens the harbor; the lighthouse ledger is donated to the archive. Beat: the town learns to keep honest minutes.

chapters.title: Salt, Then Sweet
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Theo's voice at last in first person: she cooks her mother's recipe, tastes every layer — grief, love, duty, release — and writes the dedication: 'For the ones who waited by the water.' Beat: resolution; love outlasting duty, belonging earned through truth.
